*   **Local Muscular Endurance:** A high repetition scheme with light loads (15+ repetitions per set, using loads below 60% of 1RM) is proposed to optimize improvements in local muscular endurance, which is the ability of a muscle or group of muscles to sustain repeated contractions against a resistance [Schoenfeld et al., 2021, p. 2].

This theory is based on early work by DeLorme, who suggested that heavy loads build strength and light loads build endurance, with each loading zone being unable to achieve the adaptations of the other. Subsequent research by Anderson and Kearney (1982) and Stone et al. (1994) provided some support for this hypothesis, forming the basis of the commonly accepted theory [Schoenfeld et al., 2021, p. 2].

**Challenges to the Traditional View by Recent Research:**

Emerging research challenges various aspects of the repetition continuum, suggesting that muscular adaptations can be achieved, and sometimes optimized, across a wider range of loading zones than traditionally believed [Schoenfeld et al., 2021, Abstract, p. 1; Schoenfeld et al., 2021, p. 2].

Specifically, for **muscular endurance**, research has shown conflicting findings:

*   **Maximal Voluntary Contraction (MVC):** This measures the maximum strength a muscle can produce, either isometrically (without movement) or isokinetically (at a constant speed) [Pearson et al., 2023, p. 1].

*   **Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS):** This is the aching pain felt in a muscle after a new or intense exercise. While commonly experienced, DOMS is not necessarily a direct indicator of the *amount* of muscle damage [Pearson et al., 2023, p. 1; Cintineo et al., 2018, p. 3].
*   **Whole Body Protein Metabolism:** This includes measures like whole body protein breakdown, synthesis, and net protein balance. *   **Role of Carbohydrates (CHO):** Early research focused on acute carbohydrate ingestion to replenish glycogen stores, which are depleted during moderate- and high-intensity aerobic exercise [Arent et al., 2020, p. 1]. *   **Role of Protein (PRO):** Protein intake, particularly essential amino acids (EAA) like leucine, has been emphasized for significantly increasing muscle protein synthesis (MPS) after resistance exercise [Arent et al., 2020, p. 2].
